title: The Religious Development of the Jews
orientation: Russell opens Book Two by asking what, exactly, Christianity inherited from Judaism before it became a Greco-Roman phenomenon. This chapter traces the historical development of Israelite religion from tribal henotheism to the exclusive, universalist monotheism of the prophets, the Law, and apocalyptic hope, arguing that specific historical crises (conquest, exile, persecution) forged the ideas of sacred history, a chosen people, and reward/punishment after death that Christianity would later absorb and reinterpret. Understanding this background matters because, for Russell, Christian theology cannot be understood as a purely Greek philosophical product; it is a fusion of Platonic/Stoic metaphysics with a distinctly Jewish conception of history and morals.
historical_background: Russell sketches Jewish political history from the divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah, through the Assyrian conquest of Israel (722 B.C.) and the Babylonian conquest of Judah and destruction of the Temple (586 B.C.), the Babylonian Captivity, the Persian-sponsored return under Cyrus (537 B.C.) and the work of Ezra and Nehemiah, the Hellenistic period following Alexander's conquests, the Seleucid king Antiochus IV's persecution and forced Hellenization (from 175 B.C.), the Maccabean revolt and the Hasmonean dynasty, Roman client-kingship under Herod, the destruction of the Second Temple in A.D. 70, and the growth of the Jewish Diaspora, especially the large, hellenized Jewish community of Alexandria.
philosophical_problems: What did Christianity actually inherit from Judaism, as distinct from what it derived from Greek philosophy or Near Eastern mystery cults?
How did exclusive monotheism ('no other gods') emerge historically out of an earlier tribal henotheism that tolerated other peoples' gods?
How does the problem of the virtuous suffering unjustly (national defeat, persecution) generate the belief in reward and punishment after death?
What is the relationship between ritual/legal identity (the Law) and the survival of a religious-national community under foreign domination?
How does a 'this-worldly,' concrete conception of a future golden age or afterlife differ from the Greek philosophical conception of an eternal, non-temporal reality?
Why did a persecuted minority develop a psychology of collective, and later individual, sin as an explanation for suffering?

philosophers_discussed.name: Jeremiah
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited by Russell as one of the prophets who, shortly before the Babylonian captivity, first taught that worship of other gods is sin and that Yahweh punishes idolatry -- an innovation, not an ancient orthodoxy.

philosophers_discussed.name: Ezekiel
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited alongside Jeremiah as co-inventor of the doctrine that all religions but one are false and that the Lord punishes idolatry; Russell quotes his visions condemning idolatrous practices among the Jews.

philosophers_discussed.name: Deutero-Isaiah
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Identified by Russell as the author of the second half of the Book of Isaiah, 'the most remarkable of the prophets,' the first to have the Lord declare 'There is no god but I,' and the source of the messianic texts later used by Christians as prophecies of Christ.

philosophers_discussed.name: Philo
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Introduced as a contemporary of Christ and the best illustration of Greek influence on Jewish thought: an orthodox Jew in religion but a Platonist in philosophy, whose synthesis of Greek philosophy with Hebrew scripture the later Christian Fathers would follow.

core_concepts.name: Sacred history
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The idea that history is not just a record of events but a story with a beginning (Creation), a meaning, and a future goal, in which God's purposes are worked out through a particular people.
core_concepts.precise_definition: A providential narrative of history, beginning with the Creation and moving toward a future consummation, that justifies 'the ways of God to man' and treats historical events as episodes in a divine plan.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It gave Christianity (and, in Russell's view, the Jewish tradition it inherited) a linear, purposeful view of time in place of the cyclical views common in Greek and other ancient thought, and it made suffering and defeat interpretable rather than meaningless.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed and crystallized among the Jews, especially during and after the Babylonian captivity, as they reinterpreted their national catastrophes as part of a coherent divine story.
examples: The Old Testament narrative from Creation through the Exile and return
Apocalyptic literature such as the Book of Enoch projecting sacred history into the future (New Jerusalem, resurrection, Messiah)
competing_positions: Greek/Platonic view that the truly real is timeless and unchanging, so that temporal history as such has no ultimate metaphysical significance
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell later argues (in his discussion of Saint Augustine's City of God) that this Jewish pattern of sacred history was adapted wholesale by Christianity and, in secularized form, even structures modern political eschatologies such as Marxism.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly religious and political: it explained why a small, often-conquered nation still believed itself central to a cosmic plan.

core_concepts.name: The Chosen People / doctrine of election
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The belief that God has picked out one group of people for special love and a special destiny, even though they may suffer greatly in the present.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that a small section of mankind is specially loved and chosen by God; for the Jews this was the nation of Israel, for Christians it became 'the elect.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It let a small, frequently defeated nation retain a sense of unique importance and purpose, and it supplied Christianity with its own doctrine of an elect community destined for salvation.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Rooted in early tribal religion but sharpened into an exclusive doctrine during and after the Babylonian exile, alongside the new insistence on ritual and legal separateness.
examples: Israel as Yahweh's chosen nation despite conquest and exile
The Christian doctrine of 'the elect' predestined to salvation
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Carried directly into Christian theology (discussed further in Chapters II and IV), where the Church replaces the Jewish nation as the community of the elect.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Underpinned Jewish national pride under foreign domination and, later, underpinned Christian claims to exclusive religious truth.

core_concepts.name: Exclusive monotheism as a historical innovation
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Russell argues that the strict belief that there is only one true God, and that worshipping any other god is sinful, was not the original Israelite religion but was invented by the prophets shortly before the Babylonian exile.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine, first fully articulated by prophets such as Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Deutero-Isaiah, that Yahweh alone is God, that other gods either do not exist or are false, and that their worship is punishable sin -- as opposed to earlier practice in which Yahweh was one tribal god among others.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It marks, for Russell, the decisive theological turning point that separates later Judaism (and Christianity and Islam after it) from the polytheism/henotheism common in the ancient Near East.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Emerging in the period immediately before the Babylonian captivity, according to Russell's reading of the earlier prophetic texts, and reinforced by the trauma of exile.
examples: The First Commandment ('Thou shalt have none other gods but me') as, in Russell's reading, a contemporary innovation rather than ancient law
Jeremiah's and Ezekiel's denunciations of Jews worshipping the 'queen of heaven' and the sun
objections: The Old Testament's own historical books present idolatry as a falling-off from an earlier strict monotheism, which Russell argues is a misleading retrospective compiled after the exile
competing_positions: The traditional/orthodox theological view that strict monotheism was revealed from the beginning rather than developed historically
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Became foundational to Christianity and, through it and Judaism, to Islam.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly religious, but also political: it hardened Jewish identity against both foreign conquerors and hellenizing assimilation.

core_concepts.name: The Law as identity and survival
core_concepts.plain_explanation: After the destruction of the Temple and during the exile, Jewish religious practice shifted toward the Law (circumcision, dietary rules, the Sabbath, avoidance of intermarriage) as the marks that held the nation together without a central temple or state.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The body of ritual, ceremonial, and ethical rules attributed to Moses, elevated during and after the exile into the central marker of Jewish identity and the chief unifying force of a scattered or subjugated nation.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It let Jewish identity survive the loss of political independence and the Temple, but Russell notes it also produced a rigid, conservative religious culture that later suppressed prophetic innovation.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Intensified during the Babylonian captivity (synagogues, Sabbath emphasis, circumcision as 'the mark of the Jew,' prohibition of intermarriage) and further hardened after the persecution of Antiochus IV.
examples: The Maccabean martyrs who died rather than eat pork or abandon circumcision
Ezra and Nehemiah's dissolution of mixed marriages on return from exile
competing_positions: Saint Paul's later revolt against the domination of the Law in early Christianity (previewed by Russell at the end of this chapter)
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Christianity kept parts of the Law (e.g., the Decalogue) while rejecting its ceremonial and ritual parts, substituting devotion to the Creed for devotion to the Law.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Central to both religious observance and Jewish national survival under successive empires.

core_concepts.name: Belief in reward and punishment after death
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The idea that if good people suffer and bad people prosper in this life, justice must be completed after death, with the virtuous rewarded and the wicked punished.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine of personal immortality and post-mortem reward/punishment, which Russell says became widely accepted among Jews specifically during the persecution of Antiochus IV, when virtue and martyrdom were not rewarded on earth.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It solved a theological problem (theodicy): if Yahweh is just and all-powerful and yet the virtuous are tortured and killed, justice must be reserved for another world.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Widely adopted during the Maccabean persecution (2nd century B.C.); not universal even then, since the Sadducees continued to reject it into the time of Christ.
examples: The martyrdoms recounted in 1 and 4 Maccabees, where victims affirm eternal bliss awaits them and eternal torment awaits their persecutor
competing_positions: The earlier view, reflected in older parts of the Old Testament, that virtue is rewarded and vice punished within this life
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Passed into Christianity as a central doctrine and, according to Russell, into the New Testament's concrete, temporal conception of the 'Kingdom of Heaven.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: A direct religious response to the political experience of persecution and defeat.

core_concepts.name: The Messiah
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The hope for a future deliverer who would set things right for the chosen people.
core_concepts.precise_definition: For Jews, a future figure who would bring temporal prosperity and victory over enemies on earth; for Christians, this hope was historicized and identified with Jesus, also merged with the Greek philosophical idea of the Logos, and relocated to a heavenly rather than earthly triumph.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It shows the transformation of a this-worldly Jewish political hope into an other-worldly Christian theological doctrine.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Rooted in prophetic texts, especially those of Deutero-Isaiah, later read by Christians as predictions of Christ.
examples: Isaiah's prophecies of the 'Prince of Peace' and the suffering servant of Isaiah 53
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Central to Christian theology from the outset (Chapter II).
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Originally a political hope for national deliverance, later theologized.

core_concepts.name: The Kingdom of Heaven / concrete other-worldliness
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Unlike Greek philosophers, who imagined a timeless, purely intellectual 'real' world behind the world of appearances, Jews and Christians imagined a literal future world -- a future time when the good will be rewarded and the wicked punished.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The Jewish and Christian doctrine that the 'Other World' is not metaphysically different from this world but lies in the future, when the virtuous will enjoy everlasting bliss and the wicked will suffer everlasting torment -- a concrete, temporal other-worldliness rather than the Greek philosophers' atemporal metaphysical one.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell argues this concrete, revenge-inflected doctrine was 'intelligible to all and sundry,' unlike the abstract doctrines of Greek philosophers, and this popular intelligibility helped Christianity spread.
core_concepts.historical_origin: A Jewish elaboration of older Near Eastern and Persian-influenced ideas about an afterlife, sharpened during persecution.
examples: The Book of Enoch's vivid descriptions of heaven, hell, and the Last Judgement
competing_positions: Platonic doctrine that the sensible world in space and time is illusion and that the eternal, non-temporal world alone is real
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Shapes popular Christian eschatology throughout the Middle Ages, as distinct from more Platonized theological Christianity.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Religious doctrine with an emotional root Russell calls 'revenge psychology.'

arguments.title: The theodicy of captivity: suffering as paternal correction
arguments.philosopher: Jewish prophetic tradition (as reconstructed by Russell)
premises: The Jews are Yahweh's specially chosen people.
The Jews nevertheless suffered catastrophic defeat and exile.
arguments.conclusion: Their suffering can only be explained by their own wickedness (idolatry, failure to keep the Law); the captivity is Yahweh's paternal punishment meant to purify them.
arguments.explanation: Russell presents this as the psychological mechanism by which a devastating national defeat was made compatible with continued belief in a benevolent, all-powerful, and specially favoring God: rather than doubt Yahweh's power or love, the Jews concluded they themselves must be at fault, which in turn justified the prophets' demand for stricter religious exclusivity and observance.
implications: It produced a much more rigid and nationally exclusive orthodoxy in exile than had existed before it
It set a psychological pattern -- suffering as evidence of sin, or as a test -- that recurs in Christian theology of sin and grace

arguments.title: The theodicy of persecution: immortality as compensation for injustice on earth
arguments.philosopher: Jewish tradition during the Maccabean period (as reconstructed by Russell)
premises: It was believed that virtue would be rewarded here on earth.
Persecution under Antiochus IV fell precisely upon the most virtuous and law-observant Jews.
Divine justice must ultimately be vindicated.
arguments.conclusion: Therefore rewards and punishments must occur after death, since they evidently do not occur reliably during life.
arguments.explanation: Russell treats this as a second, later theodicy, distinct from the exile-era one: instead of blaming the sufferers, this argument preserves both divine justice and the innocence of the martyrs by moving the reckoning to an afterlife, producing the doctrine of personal immortality that became near-universal among Jews (though the Sadducees held out against it) and passed into Christianity.
implications: Belief in personal immortality became central not only to later Judaism but to Christian doctrine
It reframes martyrdom as guaranteed future triumph rather than mere loss

key_distinctions: Henotheism (Yahweh as one god among others) vs. exclusive monotheism (Yahweh as the only God)
Sacrificial Temple worship vs. non-sacrificial synagogue worship (forced by the Temple's destruction)
Concrete, future, this-world-continuous 'Other World' (Jewish/Christian) vs. timeless, metaphysically separate eternal world (Greek/Platonic)
Collective/national sin (pre-exilic and early post-exilic) vs. individual sin (a later development, important for Christian theology)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell draws a sharp contrast, rather than a connection, between Jewish religious thought and earlier Greek philosophy: where Greek philosophers (especially Plato) located ultimate reality in a timeless, non-sensory realm, Jewish and Christian thought placed the 'Other World' concretely in the future, within history. He briefly quotes Empedocles to illustrate the Greek capacity for this-worldly joy that he contrasts with the later, gloomier religious mood.
connections_to_later_philosophers: This chapter sets up Chapter II's account of how Jewish sacred history, election, the Law, and messianism combined with Greek philosophy (via Philo's precedent and later the Christian Fathers) to form Christian theology. Russell also flags that Philo's Platonizing interpretation of Judaism directly anticipated the Christian Fathers' project of reconciling Greek philosophy with the Hebrew Scriptures, and that the pattern of sacred history discussed here recurs, secularized, in his later discussion of Marx's eschatology (Chapter IV).
political_social_context: The chapter is structured around successive imperial dominations of the Jews -- Assyrian, Babylonian, Persian, Macedonian/Hellenistic (Ptolemaic and Seleucid), Roman -- and shows how religious doctrine hardened in response to each crisis: the Assyrian and Babylonian conquests produced exclusive monotheism and the Law; Antiochus IV's Hellenizing persecution produced martyrdom and belief in immortality and provoked the Maccabean revolt; Roman client rule under Herod and the later revolt of A.D. 66 led to the destruction of the Temple and the definitive turn to Diaspora Judaism. Russell also notes the much better treatment of Jews under medieval Islamic rule (e.g., Moorish Spain, Maimonides) compared with medieval Christendom's persecutions and pogroms.
religion_science_culture_context: Covers the emergence of the synagogue as a substitute for Temple sacrifice, the translation of the Hebrew Bible into Greek (the Septuagint) for the hellenized Alexandrian Jewish community and its later supersession, within Judaism, by a return to the Hebrew text; the apocalyptic literature of the Book of Enoch and its influence on New Testament ideas of Messiah, hell, and demonology; and the philosophy of Philo as the first major fusion of Jewish scripture with Greek (chiefly Platonic) philosophy.
russell_presentation: Russell treats Jewish religious history as a historically explicable, evolving human phenomenon rather than as a continuous revealed truth: he explicitly argues that exclusive monotheism, hostility to other religions, and belief in personal immortality were historical innovations forged by specific prophets and specific crises (exile, persecution), not eternal or original Israelite doctrine, and he criticizes the Old Testament's historical books for retrospectively projecting later strictness onto earlier periods. His overall tone toward the Jews of this period is admiring of their 'stubborn national pride' and heroism under persecution (the Maccabean martyrs), while being frankly critical of aspects he finds unattractive -- the harsh treatment of slaves and women in Ecclesiasticus, the vengeful tone of apocalyptic writers such as the author of Enoch, and the narrow exclusivism produced by rigid devotion to the Law. He credits the Jews with contributing sacred history, the doctrine of election, an emphasis on almsgiving/practical philanthropy, and (via prophets such as Deutero-Isaiah) messianic texts central to Christian apologetics, while distinguishing these from elements he traces to Greek philosophy or to Near Eastern mystery cults. He also singles out, approvingly, the comparatively humane treatment of Jews under medieval Islamic rule as against Christian persecution.
critical_context: Later biblical and historical scholarship (source criticism, the documentary hypothesis, and comparative Near Eastern religious history) has broadly supported Russell's central claim that strict, exclusive monotheism developed gradually rather than being original to earliest Israelite religion, though scholars continue to debate the precise dating, mechanisms, and regional variation of this development more cautiously than Russell's compressed narrative suggests. This is a matter of ongoing historical-critical scholarship, separate from traditional religious readings of the same texts, which understand the same material through revelation rather than historical evolution; Russell's presentation in this chapter is explicitly the secular historical-critical one, not a theological claim about revealed truth.
key_takeaways: Russell identifies six specifically Jewish elements absorbed into Christianity: sacred history, the doctrine of a chosen/elect people, an emphasis on almsgiving and practical righteousness, an attitude to law/creed paralleling the Jewish Law, the doctrine of the Messiah, and a concrete this-worldly conception of the Kingdom of Heaven.
Exclusive monotheism ('no other gods') was, in Russell's reading, a historical innovation of the prophets shortly before the Babylonian exile, not the original religion of the Israelites.

National catastrophe (exile, persecution) repeatedly generated new theological solutions: exile produced a stricter, more exclusive orthodoxy and the Law as an identity marker; persecution under Antiochus IV produced belief in personal immortality as compensation for unjust suffering.
The Maccabean revolt against Antiochus IV's forced Hellenization was, in Russell's judgment, historically decisive: without it, Judaism (and later Christianity and Islam) might not have survived.

Hellenistic Judaism, especially in Alexandria, produced the Septuagint and, in Philo, the first major attempt to fuse Jewish scripture with Greek (Platonic) philosophy -- a precedent the Christian Fathers would follow.

Russell contrasts the concrete, future-oriented Jewish/Christian 'Other World' with the timeless, metaphysical Greek conception of ultimate reality, arguing the former's intelligibility to ordinary people helped it spread more widely than philosophical doctrines.
study_notes:
This chapter functions as a kind of prologue to all of Book Two: before Russell can explain how 'Catholic philosophy' fused Platonism with Christian doctrine, he has to isolate what, in that fusion, is neither Platonic nor generically religious but specifically Jewish. It helps to read the chapter as answering one question repeatedly: when the ordinary run of ancient religion (tribal gods, temple sacrifice, this-life rewards) failed to fit lived experience -- conquest, exile, persecution -- what new doctrines did Jewish religious leaders invent to make sense of it, and which of those doctrines did Christianity later keep? Notice the pattern: crisis, followed by theological innovation, followed by that innovation becoming the new orthodoxy. This is worth tracking because Russell will use the same analytical move throughout Book Two (for instance with Saint Augustine's City of God, written to explain the fall of Rome).

A second thread worth separating out is the tension between particularism and universalism. Much of the chapter's Jewish material is defiantly particularist -- the Law, circumcision, dietary rules, and endogamy exist precisely to keep the community distinct from surrounding peoples. But strands within the same tradition (Deutero-Isaiah's prophecies that 'the gentiles shall come to thy light,' the ethical universalism of the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs) point toward a more universal religion. Russell's account of Saint Paul's later 'revolt against the domination of the Law' (previewed at the very end of this chapter and developed in Chapter II) makes far more sense once you see that Christianity resolved this internal Jewish tension by keeping the universalist, prophetic strand and discarding the particularist, legal one.

Finally, be alert to the difference between Russell's historical claims (which are contestable and were controversial in his own day) and his own evaluative commentary. He is not simply reporting; he is offering a specific, secular, historical-critical account of how Jewish religion developed, and he does not hide his personal judgments -- admiration for Maccabean heroism, distaste for Ecclesiasticus's misogyny, or approval of medieval Islamic tolerance toward Jews as against Christian persecution.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The name of the God of Israel in the Hebrew Bible.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The tetragrammaton-derived name for the Israelite deity, originally, per Russell's account, one tribal god among several regional gods before becoming, through prophetic reinterpretation, the sole God.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The belief that God picked out one group for special favor and a special role in history.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The doctrine of divine election of a specific people (Israel) or, in Christian adaptation, a specific community ('the elect') as objects of God's particular love and salvific purpose.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The body of religious rules -- like keeping the Sabbath, avoiding certain foods, and circumcision -- that mark someone as Jewish.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The Mosaic Law (Torah), comprising ethical, ceremonial, and ritual precepts, which took on heightened importance as a marker of national-religious identity during and after the Babylonian exile.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Jewish communities living outside the land of Israel, scattered across the ancient world.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The dispersion of Jewish populations beyond Judea/Palestine, especially following the Babylonian exile and subsequent conquests, notably including large, hellenized communities such as that of Alexandria.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: An ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, made for Greek-speaking Jews.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures produced in Alexandria beginning in the mid-third century B.C. (the Pentateuch first), later relied upon heavily by early (mostly non-Hebrew-reading) Christians, though later shown by scholarship to differ significantly from the Hebrew original.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A pious, traditionalist Jewish party that resisted Greek cultural influence and Antiochus IV's persecution.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A party of strict religious observance ('the Holy') strong among the rural population of Judea in the 2nd century B.C., forerunners, per Russell, of both the Pharisees and possibly the Essenes.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A Jewish religious group known for strict devotion to the Law, out of which some strands of early Christian ethics arguably grew.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A Jewish religious-political party descended from the Hasidim, emphasizing strict adherence to the Law; Russell notes that, while later Christian tradition views Pharisees negatively, some Pharisaic ethical writing (e.g., the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs) closely anticipates the ethics of the Gospels.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A Jewish religious-political group, prominent among the priestly aristocracy, that rejected belief in an afterlife.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A Jewish sect, largely drawn from the priestly and aristocratic class, that rejected the doctrine of personal immortality even after it had become widespread among other Jews by the time of Christ.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Jewish religious writings from around the time of the Old and New Testaments that were not included in the official Hebrew Bible, such as Ecclesiasticus and the Book of Enoch.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Bodies of Second Temple-period Jewish literature excluded from the Hebrew canon (Apocrypha, e.g., Ecclesiasticus, 1-4 Maccabees) or falsely attributed to ancient authorities (Pseudepigrapha, e.g., the Book of Enoch), important as evidence for the development of Jewish thought immediately before Christianity.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, what six elements did Christianity take from Judaism?
questions.answer: Sacred history; the doctrine of a chosen/elect people; a new conception of righteousness centered on almsgiving; an attitude toward the Law paralleled by Christian attachment to the Creed; the doctrine of the Messiah; and a concrete, future-oriented conception of the Kingdom of Heaven.
questions.explanation: Russell lists these explicitly at the start of the chapter as the specifically Jewish contribution to Christianity, distinct from its Greek philosophical and Near Eastern mystery-cult elements.

questions.prompt: Why does Russell argue that strict, exclusive monotheism was not the original religion of the Israelites?
questions.answer: Russell points to earlier prophetic texts showing that worship of other gods (such as the 'queen of heaven') was habitual among Israelites before the exile, and argues that Jeremiah and Ezekiel appear to have invented the idea that all other religions are false and that Yahweh punishes idolatry, an innovation shortly before the Babylonian captivity.
questions.explanation: This is central to Russell's historical-critical reading: he treats the Old Testament's presentation of earlier idolatry as a 'falling-off' from strictness as a misleading retrospective compiled after the exile.

questions.prompt: Which figure does Russell describe as an orthodox Jew in religion but 'primarily a Platonist' in philosophy, whose approach the Christian Fathers later followed?
questions.explanation: Philo, a contemporary of Christ living in Alexandria, combined orthodox Jewish religious practice with a Platonist (and Stoic/Neopythagorean-influenced) philosophy, showing later Christian thinkers how to reconcile Greek philosophy with acceptance of Hebrew scripture.

questions.prompt: How does the Jewish/Christian conception of the 'Other World' differ from the Greek philosophical (Platonic) conception, according to Russell?
questions.answer: The Greek/Platonic view holds that the sensible world in space and time is illusory, and that through intellectual and moral discipline a person can come to live in an eternal, metaphysically distinct world that alone is real. The Jewish and Christian view instead places the Other World in the future within this same historical timeline: a coming time when the virtuous will enjoy everlasting bliss and the wicked everlasting torment.
questions.explanation: This distinction matters for Russell's later argument (Chapter II) that the Jewish/Christian version, being 'intelligible to all and sundry,' had greater popular appeal than the abstract Platonic doctrine.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct the reasoning Russell attributes to Jews under the persecution of Antiochus IV that led to a widespread belief in personal immortality.
questions.answer: It had been believed that virtue would be rewarded on earth; but persecution fell precisely on the most virtuous and law-observant; therefore, to preserve the justice of an all-powerful God, rewards and punishments must be reserved for a life after death.
questions.explanation: Russell treats this as a distinct, later theodicy from the earlier exile-era one (which blamed the sufferers themselves); here the martyrs are innocent, so justice is deferred to the afterlife rather than earned through repentance.

questions.prompt: What historical event does Russell credit with possibly saving Judaism (and, with it, the historical possibility of Christianity and Islam) from extinction?
questions.answer: The heroic resistance of the Hasidim and the Maccabean martyrs against Antiochus IV's persecution and forced Hellenization.
questions.explanation: Russell quotes Townsend's remark that 'the blood of the Maccabean martyrs... ultimately became the seed of the Church,' underscoring how contingent later monotheistic religious history was on this 2nd-century B.C. resistance.

questions.prompt: How, according to Russell, were Jews treated differently under medieval Christian versus medieval Islamic rule?
questions.answer: Under medieval Christian rule, Jews were severely persecuted (especially during the Crusades) and largely excluded from cultural life; under Islamic rule, especially in Moorish Spain, they were treated humanely and were able to contribute significantly to learning and philosophy (e.g., Maimonides).
questions.explanation: Russell uses this contrast to make a broader point about the comparative civilization and humaneness of the medieval Islamic and Christian worlds.

flashcards.front: What are the six Jewish elements Russell says Christianity inherited from Judaism?
flashcards.back: Sacred history, the chosen/elect people, righteousness via almsgiving, an attitude to Law paralleling the Creed, the Messiah, and a concrete Kingdom of Heaven.

flashcards.front: Who does Russell credit with inventing the idea that all religions but one are false?
flashcards.back: The prophets Jeremiah and Ezekiel, shortly before the Babylonian captivity.

flashcards.front: What happened to the Northern Kingdom of Israel in 722 B.C.?
flashcards.back: It was conquered by the Assyrians, who removed much of the population.

flashcards.front: Who destroyed the Temple in 586 B.C. and took Jews captive to Babylon?
Who issued the edict allowing Jews to return to Palestine from Babylon?
flashcards.back: Cyrus, king of the Medes and Persians, in 537 B.C.

flashcards.front: What changes to Jewish religious practice did the Babylonian captivity produce?
flashcards.back: Non-sacrificial worship, the beginning of synagogues, emphasis on the Sabbath and circumcision, and prohibition of intermarriage.

flashcards.front: Who is Deutero-Isaiah and why is he significant?
flashcards.back: The author of the later chapters of the Book of Isaiah; the first prophet to declare 'There is no god but I,' and source of messianic texts central to later Christian apologetics.

flashcards.front: What did Antiochus IV try to do to the Jews starting in 175 B.C.?
flashcards.back: Forcibly hellenize them: establishing a gymnasium in Jerusalem, banning circumcision and Jewish dietary laws, and placing an image in the Temple.

flashcards.front: Who led the successful revolt against Antiochus IV?
According to Russell, why did belief in personal immortality become widespread among Jews around the Maccabean period?
flashcards.back: Because persecution fell on the most virtuous, so justice for the martyrs had to be deferred to an afterlife.

flashcards.front: Which Jewish sect continued to reject the doctrine of immortality even in the time of Christ?

flashcards.back: The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible made for Greek-speaking (Alexandrian) Jews, later heavily used by early Christians.

flashcards.front: Who is Philo and why does Russell single him out?
flashcards.back: A Jewish philosopher, contemporary of Christ, orthodox in religion but Platonist in philosophy; he showed later Christian Fathers how to reconcile Greek philosophy with Hebrew scripture.

flashcards.front: What is the Book of Enoch and why does Russell discuss it?
flashcards.back: An apocalyptic Jewish text (composite, roughly 2nd-1st century B.C.) with visions of heaven, hell, and judgment; it influenced New Testament ideas of the Messiah, Sheol, and demonology.

flashcards.front: How did Herod (King of the Jews under Rome) treat the Jewish religion?
flashcards.back: He rebuilt the Temple in Hellenistic style but placed a golden eagle over its gate, violating the Second Commandment, provoking Pharisaic opposition he then punished.

quiz.prompt: Which empire destroyed the Temple in Jerusalem in 586 B.C. and took many Jews captive?
quiz.explanation: Nebuchadrezzar of Babylon captured Jerusalem, destroyed the Temple, and removed a large part of the population to Babylon in 586 B.C.

quiz.prompt: Who issued the edict permitting Jews to return to Palestine from Babylonian captivity?
quiz.explanation: Cyrus, king of the Medes and Persians, issued the edict in 537 B.C. after conquering Babylon.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, which prophets first taught that worship of other gods was sin, shortly before the Babylonian captivity?
quiz.explanation: Russell identifies Jeremiah and Ezekiel as apparently inventing the doctrine that all religions but one are false.
quiz.related_concept: Exclusive monotheism as a historical innovation

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, the Old Testament's historical books give an accurate account of Jewish religious history, showing a strict monotheism that later declined into idolatry.
quiz.explanation: Russell argues the opposite: the historical books, mostly compiled after the captivity, give a 'misleading impression' since earlier strictness never actually existed; the prophets were innovators.
quiz.related_concept: Exclusive monotheism as a historical innovation

quiz.prompt: Which Seleucid king attempted to forcibly hellenize the Jews and provoked the Maccabean revolt?
quiz.explanation: Antiochus IV established a gymnasium in Jerusalem, banned circumcision and Jewish dietary law, and placed an image of a god in the Temple, provoking rebellion.

quiz.prompt: Why, according to Russell, did belief in personal immortality become widespread among Jews around the time of the Maccabees?
options: Persecution fell upon the most virtuous, requiring justice to be reserved for an afterlife
Greek philosophers converted the Jewish priesthood
It had always been the official doctrine of the Temple
quiz.explanation: Since virtue was not rewarded in this life for the martyrs, divine justice required belief in rewards and punishments after death.
quiz.related_concept: Belief in reward and punishment after death

quiz.prompt: Russell calls Philo the best illustration of Greek influence on Jewish thought because, while orthodox in religion, he was primarily a ______ in philosophy.
quiz.explanation: Philo was primarily a Platonist, with important Stoic and Neopythagorean influences as well.

quiz.prompt: Which Jewish sect still rejected the doctrine of immortality at the time of Christ, according to Russell?
quiz.explanation: The Sadducees continued to reject the belief in personal immortality even by the time of Christ, though by then they were a small party.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, under which medieval rule were Jews treated more humanely and able to contribute to philosophy and learning?
options: Under Christian rule during the Crusades
Under Islamic rule, especially in Moorish Spain
quiz.explanation: Russell notes Jews were treated humanely under Islamic rule, particularly in Moorish Spain, where figures like Maimonides flourished, in contrast to persecution under medieval Christendom.

quiz.prompt: Match each figure to their role: (1) Deutero-Isaiah, (2) Philo, (3) Judas Maccabaeus, (4) Ezra and Nehemiah -- with (A) led the revolt against Antiochus IV, (B) led the return from exile and enforced dissolution of mixed marriages, (C) first prophet to declare 'There is no god but I', (D) fused Jewish scripture with Platonist philosophy.
quiz.explanation: Deutero-Isaiah (C), Philo (D), Judas Maccabaeus (A), Ezra and Nehemiah (B).

essay_prompts.prompt: Russell argues that key Jewish doctrines -- exclusive monotheism, the Law, and belief in personal immortality -- arose as historical responses to specific national crises (exile, persecution) rather than being original or timeless. Analyze this argument using at least two of the theodicies discussed in the chapter, and assess how convincing you find the historical-critical explanation as opposed to a purely theological one.
rubric: Correctly reconstructs at least two theodicies (exile-era and persecution-era)
Distinguishes Russell's Layer 1 historical argument from a theological counter-reading
Provides a reasoned assessment, not just summary

essay_prompts.prompt: Compare the Jewish/Christian conception of the 'Other World' as a future, concrete state within history with the Greek/Platonic conception of an eternal, non-temporal reality behind appearances. What consequences does Russell suggest this difference had for the spread of Christianity?
rubric: Draws out the popular-intelligibility point Russell makes
Connects the comparison to Christianity's later success (as previewed at the end of the chapter)
Uses specific textual examples (e.g., Book of Enoch vs. Platonic doctrine)
